summary: Beacon on a rock in the St. Lawrence River near Alexandria Bay, lit from 1847; its iron tower dates from 1882. Still lit and solar-powered, but closed to visitors.

structures.type: round iron tower lined with brick
structures.note: Replaced the 1847 brick tower on the same foundation

access.note: Tower and grounds closed; seen from the shore at Alexandria Bay and from tour boats.

events.note: Brick beacon built atop the rock on a protective pier, after the March 1847 appropriation
Five lamps in reflectors gave a fixed white light until 1855
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors
Brick tower torn down May 15, 1882; new iron tower exhibited June 12, 1882
At the opening of navigation the light changed from white to red and the tower from brown to white
Horace E. Walts transferred from an assistant's post at Oswego to head keeper
Keeper Frederick Lawson commended for rescuing a boy from drowning
Food and shelter for two men whose power boat had drifted (April 27)
Walts rescued a man from a skiff on August 6 (the Bulletin's 1914 volume); LighthouseFriends dates it to 1916
Fixed red changed to fixed green
Electrified November 21, 1934; intensity raised to 1,500 candlepower
Walts resigned in July 1937 for poor health; Edward J. Sweet made responsible for this and several other automated lights

keepers.name: Frederick Lawson
keepers.note: Commended in 1912 for rescuing a boy from drowning.

keepers.name: Horace E. Walts
keepers.note: Came from an assistant's post at Oswego. Inspector's efficiency star for nine consecutive years (LighthouseFriends). Son Max recalled rowing out with him. Rescues 1914.

wrecks.outcome: Struck Pullman Shoal after passing Sunken Rock in poor visibility; beached near the Coast Guard station on Wellesley Island and sank before dawn. Now a dive site. Passed the light; not at it.

corrections.why: The 1847 tower was a brick beacon torn down on May 15, 1882. The iron tower standing now was exhibited on June 12, 1882 (LighthouseFriends; Thousand Islands Life quoting the Board).
LighthouseFriends describes the 1882 tower as a round iron tower lined with brick to the first landing. Our sources do not confirm 'cast iron'.
The archive gives the light at 27.75 feet above mean high water (about 8.5 m).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1848 as the year the station was established. LighthouseFriends and Thousand Islands Life date the brick beacon to the summer of 1847, after the March 1847 appropriation. The record keeps 1847 as the first light.
Two of our sources give the 1847 tower as brick and the iron tower as 1882. Rowlett's directory gives 1884 for a second tower; neither source supports that date, so the story uses 1882.
The Bulletin's 1914 volume records the August 6 skiff rescue; LighthouseFriends dates it to 1916. The story keeps the Bulletin's 1914 year until the issue date is checked.

notes_for_editor: The story runs about 900 words. That is the length the evidence supports: the core facts come from one LighthouseFriends page, one Thousand Islands Life page and four primary Board and Bulletin pages, and nothing was padded. The archive's Sunken Rock record gives a cast-iron tower built 1847 and a 1848 establishment year; LighthouseFriends and Thousand Islands Life say the 1847 tower was brick and the iron tower dates from 1882 (see corrections). The Board's 1878, 1880 and 1882 reports are read through Thousand Islands Life and LighthouseFriends, because the corpus Board volumes start in 1891. The 1904 letter is LighthouseFriends' quotation of the Board's 1905 and 1906 reports; the original was not read. Walts's skiff rescue: the Bulletin's 1914 volume (PDF page 36) gives August 6 with no year in the printed line; LighthouseFriends gives 1916; check the issue date before publication. The Commissioner's 1915 table (scan page 68, printed page 63) lists 'H. E. Walts, keeper, Sunken Rock Light Station, N. Y.' among aid to vessels; it is an OCR table read by position, so it is not used in the story. The record's characteristic 'Fl G 4s' is not supported by any source we read; LighthouseFriends says fixed green since 1931 and gives no current characteristic. A Coast Guard Light List check is needed. The Lighthouse Directory (ibiblio) entry gives 'Owner/site manager: private' and a different ARLHS number, and was not used. Wikipedia says the light is maintained by the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation under an agreement with the Coast Guard; leads only, not cited. The archive names the last keeper Edward J. Sweet; LighthouseFriends calls him Edward Sweet, Jr. Thousand Islands Life's keeper table gives Sweet 1937-1958 against the archive's and LighthouseFriends' 1960; the story states both. The LighthouseFriends distance is 'about half a mile below Alexandria Bay' while Thousand Islands Life says 'half a mile north'; the story avoids the direction. The Roy A. Jodrey wreck comes from LighthouseFriends alone; no Coast Guard or NTSB record was read. The keeper's son's recollection is as LighthouseFriends prints it.
